A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching objectives, algorithms, and theoretical results. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix H report original simulations on normal-form and grid-world Stag Hunt, Matching Pennies, and multi-agent cooperative games.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G retain original steering experiments and report a revised large-model experiment involving avaricious agents.

M1.justification: Objective (1), belief-state steering, FETE, and Algorithms 3–4 retain their procedures. The posterior-based exploration objective numbered (13) in v2 already appears unnumbered in v1 Appendix H.3.2. The revised agent dynamics belong to the experimental environment.

E1.justification: Section 6.2 replaces the large-model scenario of intrinsically rewarded, opportunistic agents that accelerate learning with larger action-value differences. The replacement uses agents with no intrinsic rewards whose learning slows under high incentive payments, with the mediator rewarded for unanimous action A. The other game environments remain.

E2.justification: Figure 3 adds FETE-RE to the final steering-gap and cost comparisons, which previously included only FETE and Oracle. Random exploration already appeared in the identification comparison. FETE-RE is explicitly an adaptation of SIAR-MPC using MLE and RL, rather than an evaluation of its original implementation.

E3.justification: The revised large-model evaluation changes the candidate class from 4^10 to 3^10, Umax from 2.0 to 1.0, and the evaluated realizations from four to three. Figure 3 changes whole-model identification probability to agent-type identification accuracy and plots steering gap divided by N. The 500-step total horizon and 30-step exploration budget remain.

E4.justification: The FETE versus FETE-RE comparison extends the exploration analysis to downstream steering gaps and costs, holding the identification and exploitation approach fixed. Previously, learned and random exploration were compared only through identification success. The existing beta-sensitivity analyses in Figures 5–6 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: The reported five-seed averaging, 95% confidence intervals, and two-sigma error-bar practices are retained, including for the revised large-model evaluation. No new statistical testing or increased run count is reported.

E6.justification: Figure 3 replaces results for fA–fD with results for f1–f3 under different agent dynamics and metrics, and adds FETE-RE outcomes. The new comparison shows larger steering gaps for FETE-RE, most visibly for f2. These are replacement results, not comparable-setting performance gains. The small-model table and Figures 1, 2, 5, and 6 retain their results.

T1.justification: The formal problem definitions, Assumptions A–D, Proposition 3.3, existence results, and PMD, MLE, and POMDP arguments are retained. Matching the renumbered appendices reveals no substantive change to their proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract newly emphasizes Markovian agents as a new general category motivated by limitations of prior work. The introduction adds a novelty claim about abstracting limited cognitive abilities and recency bias in steering. The central objective, existence, and algorithmic contribution claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds a behavioral rationale for Markovian agents and explains how insufficient exploration can confuse avaricious and normal agents, harming subsequent steering. Appendix G.4 qualifies the SIAR-MPC comparison through its necessary adaptation. The existing limitations discussion is unchanged and relocated from Appendix A to H.

D1.justification: V2 documents FETE-RE construction, adds an avarice-scaling rule, and includes an explicit pointer to supplementary running instructions. V1's statement about random initialization when training exploitation policies is no longer stated. The new scaling rule assigns both beta^n values to the same condition, pi^n(A) <= 0.5, leaving the intended implementation ambiguous. Repository, hardware, and timing disclosures remain.

R1.justification: The introduction adds behavioral literature on bounded rationality and recency bias. Sections 1.1 and 5.2 and Appendices B.2 and G.4 substantially expand positioning against Zhang et al. (2023) and Canyakmaz et al. (2024), distinguishing information assumptions, incentive representations, exploration, identification, and exploitation.

P1.justification: The introduction and closest-related-work discussion are substantially rewritten around behavioral motivation and comparative novelty. Opponent-shaping and episodic/non-episodic RL discussions move into the appendix, limitations move to the final appendix, and new comparison and reproducibility subsections reorganize the explanatory narrative.

P2.justification: V1's overview Table 1 is removed, while the retained empirical table is relocated and renumbered. Figure 3 is redrawn with three model groups, an additional comparator, and revised axes and caption. Other figures remain, alongside document-wide changes to title, headings, and preprint headers.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical support for strategic exploration by testing its downstream effects against FETE-RE, and clarifies the relationship to prior steering work. The gain is limited: the experiment replaces an existing scenario, the comparator adapts SIAR-MPC, and the contradictory scaling rule weakens reproducibility. With the theory and other experiments retained, the added controlled comparison supports a modest net improvement.
